rationale: The complete SGIM meeting body contains two references to strawberry tongue in one scarlet-fever abstract. Both describe appearance and neither denotes an ingestion exposure.
The encyclopedia entry uses a picture of a strawberry in a color-assignment illustration. It provides no food administration.
The veterinary glossary uses strawberry footrot for ovine dermatitis. The name does not refer to the fruit.
The veterinary glossary cross-references strawberry footrot in its pododermatitis and verrucose dermatitis entries. The term names a condition.
Strawberry clover in the glossary is Trifolium fragiferum. The mention does not identify Fragaria or edible strawberry fruit.
The matching word is part of a contributor name in the Parkinson exercise article. The intervention is sensorimotor training without a strawberry exposure.
The review cites compositional or plant responses in strawberries under elevated carbon dioxide. The tested exposure is the growing environment.
The original bird study administers tryptophan. Strawberries are discussed as a dietary melatonin source and are not the assigned exposure.
The review describes fisetin in strawberries and summarizes isolated-compound mechanisms. The underlying exposure is not whole raw fruit.
Strawberry appears as a candidate answer for an odor-identification item. The adaptation does not evaluate strawberry ingestion or falls.
The review cites early strawberry-supplementation rodent research. It supplies a trail to the original aging experiments and no Parkinson fall rate.
The food-supply article identifies strawberry in crop or production examples. Its data do not link intake to symptom outcomes.
The biomarker review cites strawberry addition with fasting blood oxidative measurements. The source supplies no comparison for falls.
Strawberry milk is the training reinforcer in the Huntington mouse experiment. The randomized comparison concerns cognitive training rather than raw fruit.
Strawberry is a food odor in the NHANES test battery. The measured endpoint is olfactory identification rather than a dietary intervention.
The phylogenetic article uses Fragaria vesca as a botanical outgroup. Its use is genomic context, with no measured ingestion or symptom effect.
The cardiovascular statistics report mentions strawberry tongue in Kawasaki disease. It gives no dietary strawberry or related fall comparison.
The archive of medicines advertising includes strawberry-flavored syrup. The formulation is historical context, without a dietary fruit or Parkinson falls comparison.
The review tabulates polyamines in strawberries. The constituent measurements supply neither an intake contrast nor a fall outcome.
Strawberry is among foods participants were asked to omit before circulatory measurements. The study does not compare consumption or its fall effects.
Strawberry is a sensory calibration or flavor attribute in the thickened-liquid evaluation. The panel did not study falls or regular raw fruit consumption.
The strawberry is used in a teaching analogy or demonstration of an axon terminal. There is no measured food exposure or symptom effect.
The review cites freeze-dried strawberries and fruit extracts in cancer-cell tests. It does not report a human exposure or fall outcome.
The phenotype term denotes a strawberry-shaped head in diagnostic or phenotypic discussion. It provides no food exposure.
A member of the ACNP collection uses strawberry milk as reinforcement in its mouse touchscreen task. The task manipulation does not isolate an effect of strawberry.
Either assigned group could receive strawberry or vanilla flavor. The intervention effect concerns the nutrient formula and rehabilitation gait, with no flavor-isolated fall measure.
The regional horticultural review reports actual strawberry production and composition context. It provides no measured Parkinson or falls comparison.
The review lists ellagic acid in strawberries and cites constituent experiments. Their exposures do not isolate raw fruit and its effect on falls.
Strawberry names an optimization algorithm in the methods comparison. The exposure is computational and has no food input.
The original comparative work on walnut and hazelnut bacterial strains discusses the strawberry leaf-blight pathovar. This is plant disease context.
Tables list strawberry as a familiar odor and an orange-item response choice. Neither occurrence provides a raw-food comparison.
The animal alpha-synuclein study uses strawberry milkshake as a shared touchscreen reinforcer. It compares model and protein manipulations without a food-effect contrast.
The identified fruit in the honey review is Arbutus unedo, a different genus and food from Fragaria strawberry.
The original agronomy study tests almond cultivars under water stress. Its body and references provide no strawberry exposure under the checked fruit or genus forms.
The Acer campestre risk assessment identifies strawberry host material and a fruit disease citation. These are horticultural contexts.
The original Acer pseudoplatanus commodity assessment includes strawberry in plant host or pathogen context. It measures no human outcome.
The original Acer palmatum commodity assessment lists Fragaria in pest or pathogen host material. It addresses plant-health risk rather than human symptoms.
The original Acer platanoides commodity assessment includes strawberry host material in risk and pest references, without a human exposure comparison.
The wheat biofortification review traces the GalUR gene to strawberry and discusses its expression in other crops. The original reviewed material does not test strawberry intake.
The Quercus petraea commodity assessment includes Fragaria in plant-health host or reference material without a human symptom outcome.
The Quercus robur commodity assessment includes strawberry in plant-pest host or disease references. It gives no dietary comparison.
The randomized Parkinson paper gives fall incidence by drug assignment. Both formulations used strawberry extract for taste masking, leaving no strawberry contrast or recurrent fall rate.
The reanalysis of 57 healthy adults' habitual diets includes seasonal strawberry consumption. It gives no strawberry-specific fall estimate.
The MALDI methods review cites imaging of strawberry tissue and fruit glycosides. Tissue chemistry gives no measured symptom response.
The climate impacts chapter describes wild strawberries as traditional First Foods. It gives no observed fall or Parkinson treatment comparison.
The post-COVID review includes strawberries among foods discussed for polyphenols and neurogenesis. No primary strawberry or fall comparison is reported.
The sensory procedure uses a strawberry-scented marker in odor testing for older adults with dementia. Neither food consumption nor falls are evaluated.
The review's strawberry and neurodegeneration claim points to a 2014 secondary review. It gives no original confirmation of reversal or fall outcomes for strawberry.
Strawberry tongue is a diagnostic mucosal sign in the discussion of Kawasaki disease. The body has no strawberry exposure.
The proceedings contain two strawberry-tongue descriptions in clinical assessments. They denote oral appearance, with no tested strawberry exposure.
The bifenthrin review discusses residue-risk modeling for strawberries. The potential exposure concerns the pesticide rather than an isolated strawberry effect.
The antioxidant methods review cites the original human strawberry intake paper for antioxidant measurements. It does not provide a strawberry fall result.
The review includes correspondence between strawberry odor and a color judgment. Its comparisons concern perception and report no ingestion or falls.
Strawberry milkshake is a task reinforcer in the animal synucleinopathy experiments. The comparison concerns model status or cognitive performance, without an isolated milkshake contrast.
The Huntington imaging study uses strawberry milkshake reward during training and cites the earlier training method. It gives no separate strawberry or fall comparison.
The dysphagia accessibility article names strawberry chia oats as a meal example. It assigns no menu or falls endpoint.
The plant-vesicle review discusses vesicles derived from strawberry fruit and proposed laboratory applications. It gives no raw consumption comparison.
The taste review traces strawberry and chocolate stimuli to two distinct drug fMRI studies. The compared interventions are cannabinoids and the endpoint is brain response.
The urolithin A review discusses fruit sources of ellagitannins and separable downstream products. It supplies no isolated raw-strawberry fall result.
